subtopic: PETITION WITH RESPECT TO APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE, ETC.
PETITION WITH RESPECT TO APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in accordance with standing order 70 I have a petition to present which is that of Carl Hamilton, of 155 McLeod street, city of Ottawa, county of Carleton, province of Ontario, Canada, secretary, one of the loyal subjects of Her Majesty in the right of Canada. Having perused the rules of the house with reference to this matter I find that it is my responsibility to read the petition, which I have done, and I have found that there are no irregularities, no violations of the rules and that it follows the form of petitions in every respect.
Very shortly, the petition relates to a notice of motion now standing on the order paper in the name of the Minister of Citizenship and
Immigration for the appointment of a joint committee of the House of Commons and the Senate on Indian affairs, and relates also to Bill No. C-2 standing in the name of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration and Bill No. C-3 standing in the name of the Secretary of State. It is the type of petition which is a personal one requiring immediate remedy, and comes within the provisions of standing order 70, subsection 8, of the standing orders.
If I may relate the particulars of the petition very briefly before reading the prayer in order to bring it in that way to the attention of the house, they are three in number.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: PETITION WITH RESPECT TO APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext: Order. The hon. member has the right to present the petition under standing order 70 in his place in the house, but as I read the rule it is not debatable, and I suggest that he present the petition before proceeding any further.

subtopic: PETITION WITH RESPECT TO APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext: It is not my intention to debate the petition, but inasmuch it is of the type requiring immediate action to deal with it I only wish to inform the house of what is in the petition itself. The prayer of the petition, Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: PETITION WITH RESPECT TO APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext:
Before the hon. member proceeds may I refer to standing order 70, which relates to petitions, so we may be clear that the proper procedure is being followed. Subsection 2 reads:
Any member desiring to present a petition in his place in the house must do so during routine proceedings and before the introduction of bills.
Then in subsection 3 it states:
On the presentation of a petition no debate on or in relation to the same shall be allowed.
Once a petition has been presented it is referred to the clerk of petitions and then, of course, is returned under a later section of the rule, to be reported upon.

subtopic: PETITION WITH RESPECT TO APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext:
As I pointed out initially, standing order 70, subsection 8, also makes reference to the fact that no debate shall be permitted, as you have indicated, but it also says:
-if it complains of some present personal grievance-
As this one does.
-requiring an immediate remedy-
This is one of those, that is a personal grievance requiring an immediate remedy.

Indian Affairs
-the matter contained therein may be brought into immediate discussion.
I submit that under this rule the matter may be brought into immediate discussion. It is not my intention to discuss the merits of the petition. It is only because it is one of those which I feel fall within subsection 8 of standing order 70 that I wish to give the house an indication of what it says so we may decide whether or not it should be brought forward for immediate discussion. In order to do this I would indicate what the prayer says.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PETITION WITH RESPECT TO APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext:
It
seems clear to me on reading subsection 8 of standing order 70 that any debate that can be allowed can only take place tomorrow on the report of the clerk of petitions, and not immediately on the presentation of the petition, if it is a matter requiring immediate or urgent attention. Indeed, subsection 7 says:
On the next day following the presentation of a petition the clerk of the house shall lay upon the table the report of the clerk of petitions upon the petitions presented and such report shall be printed in the Votes and Proceedings of that day-
Then subsection 8 says:
No debate shall be permitted on the report but a petition referred to therein may be read by the clerk of the house at the table, if required; or if it complain of some present personal grievance requiring an immediate remedy, the matter contained therein may be brought into immediate discussion.
It is clear, therefore, that discussion, if such discussion be in order, could not take place today but only tomorrow.

subtopic: PETITION WITH RESPECT TO APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext: With respect to the point of order raised by the Minister of Justice, I would point out that there is relatively little precedent in our rules but there is in the United Kingdom a quite extensive reference to the presentation of petitions and to bringing the matter forward for discussion immediately. I think, sir, a reference to May's "Parliamentary Rules and Practices", sixteenth edition, will show that standing order 93 is comparable to our standing order 70. You will find that the procedure is that which I suggest should be followed here, namely that there should be an immediate discussion allowed.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: PETITION WITH RESPECT TO APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext: What is the page?

subtopic: PETITION WITH RESPECT TO APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext:
It is page 1075, and deals with standing orders of the United Kingdom as they relate to petitions. They are comparable to ours and were adopted in 1842. They have been in use ever since. There is also an instance which can be found in our Canadian Journals relating to the petition of the Bishop of Ontario in 1880. I can give the reference

to Your Honour there. It is at page 130 of March 12 of that year. There is a reference to a petition which was presented that day:
And the said petition was read and received: praying that the bill now before parliament, to legalize marriage with the sister of a deceased wife, may not become law at present, but that the various religious bodies of the dominion be allowed an opportunity of expressing their convictions regarding it.
Ordered, that the said petition be printed.
It was discussed and reference was made to it at that time. I suggest this is substantially the position of this petition, in that it relates to the business of the house. It prays that some of the business of the house be speeded up, namely the motion of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, to give immediate consideration to the setting up of that joint committee; and prays, second, that Bills Nos. C-2 and C-3 be not proceeded with beyond the stage which will allow citizens outside the house to appear before the committee and present their ideas. This is substantially the position which existed in parliament in 1880 in the reference that I read.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: PETITION WITH RESPECT TO APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext:
There is a preliminary point of order, and I thank both hon. members for discussing it because it is one that does not arise very often. May I read subsection 8 of standing order 70 which has been referred to by the Minister of Justice. The procedure is, of course, that the petition, having been presented, is referred to the clerk of petitions. The next day the clerk of the house tables a report if it is in order. Up to that stage the rule says there is to be no debate. Then subsection 8 states:
No debate shall be permitted on the report-
That is the report of the clerk.
-but a petition referred to therein may be read by the clerk of the house at the table, if required; or-
And this is the part the hon. member for Skeena alleges permits him to discuss the matter today.
-if it complain of some present personal grievance-
That is the petition referred to therein.
-requiring an immediate remedy, the matter contained therein may be brought into immediate discussion.
It seems to me that the rule is clear. The practice with respect to petitions has altered greatly in recent times. At one time parliament spent much of its time receiving petitions, but now they are a rarity. There is no debate on the first presentation of a petition. The rule which the hon. member wishes to invoke in my view would only be applicable when the petition is reported and laid on the table tomorrow with the report.

But as it is a matter of novelty I think no harm is being done if I rule in that way provisionally now and consider the matter so that we may have proper authority for it and proper precedent for the future. That is the ruling I make at the present time.

subtopic: PETITION WITH RESPECT TO APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext: I should like to ask for some clarification, Mr. Speaker. Your ruling is that the petition now presented, upon a report tomorrow, may be further considered?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: PETITION WITH RESPECT TO APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE, ETC.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF ASSISTANCE TO EARTHQUAKE VICTIMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government has approved a proposal by the Canadian Red Cross Society that a donation of $20,000 be made from the international relief fund to finance emergency relief assistance to the many unfortunate victims of the terrible tragedy that struck Agadir, Morocco, earlier this week. The government has authorized the use of an R.C.A.F. aircraft to speed the dispatch to Morocco of assistance from this country.
The Canadian Red Cross, through whose willing assistance and co-operation we were able to confirm the early reports of the deaths, injuries and destruction of property, are organizing a team of medical personnel which, together with necessary equipment and supplies, will be flown to the disaster area in an R.C.A.F. aircraft.
This tragedy evokes the deepest sympathy throughout Canada, and I am sure hon. members in all parts of the house would wish to join me in expressing to the government and people of Morocco our sincere condolences.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF NEW SERIES OF SURVIVAL EXERCISES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to announce, following the planning conference of federal, provincial and Canadian army representatives in Ottawa, that a new series of civil defence survival exercises will be conducted in May.
The first of these exercises, to be known as TOCSIN, will be under the direction of the emergency measures organization. The series replaces those run in the past by the civil defence division of the Department of National Health and Welfare. TOCSIN will practise emergency arrangements for carrying on government at federal, provincial and
Proposed Legislation
municipal levels; test elements of the emergency communications system; exercise the national attack warning system down to provincial centres, and examine some of the problems to be faced following an attack.
At this stage the public will not be asked to participate actively in the exercise except in those localities where the municipalities wish to make local arrangements for this purpose. The exercise will revolve around a simulated nuclear attack on Canada by manned aircraft.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Transport. speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY WELLAND CANAL  REPRESENTATIONS RESPECTING ELIMINATION OF TOLLS
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker; on Tuesday I received a large delegation as described by the hon. member. I met with them for over two hours, and had a very thorough and useful discussion. During the discussion I pointed out to them the proceedings that had taken place in this house in 1951 when the hon.

Inquiries of the Ministry member for Laurier, as minister of transport, introduced this measure in the house on behalf of the government of that day and advised the house that it was the intention of the government to pay for the cost of building the St. Lawrence seaway which, as he described it, would extend from Montreal to lake Erie-which of course includes the Welland canal-by means of imposing tolls, and that the cost of the seaway and improvements to the Welland canal would be paid off over a period of 50 years.
I pointed out to them that this measure had been voted on by the house, had been passed by unanimous vote, and that the present government had seen no reason to change the view of the parliament of that day which had voted unanimously that the Welland canal should pay tolls the same as the rest of the St. Lawrence seaway system.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for some years the Department of National Defence has

used a standard point system for determining which employees will be released when a reduction in force becomes necessary. This system awards points for three factors, seniority, efficiency, and entitlement to the preference for war service.
The system is understood and accepted as being fair by the great majority of the department's civilian employees, and by staff associations and other employee organizations that represent them. The points given a veteran entitled to the preference are the equivalent to an additional two years' seniority. This, coupled with the preference invariably given by my department to qualified veterans at the time of employment, ensures that the rights of veterans are fully protected.
At most national defence establishments two categories of civilian staff are employed, those in continuing positions and those with casual status who are employed and released in accordance with fluctuations in the amount of work to be performed. By the very nature of their employment, casual employees are subject to lay-off on relatively short notice. Because of this, the department's lay-off system provides for the release of casual employees before a reduction in staff affects those in continuing positions. The lay-off at Point Edward naval base was confined to casual employees, with none of the staff in continuing positions being affected. This lay-off was carried out in strict accordance with departmental regulations.
Last year, as the result of a reorganization at this establishment, the continuing establishment of helper positions was reduced. A number of employees, some of them veterans, who were given the option of remaining in continuing status at the lower classification and pay of labourers or of reverting to casual status as helpers with a pay rate 8 cents per hour higher but losing their status as continuing employees in the event of a lay-off, chose the higher pay and the greater hazard of losing their jobs. The implications of this choice were explained to all the men concerned, and I do not think the department can allow them to change their options in the light of changing circumstances.
The secretary of the Cape Breton district command of the Canadian Legion appears to believe that any man entitled to the veterans preference, regardless of his seniority, should be retained in preference to any non-veteran. I am sure the hon. member will support me when I say that this proposition is not acceptable, since it would mean that a man with a few weeks' service would be
Inquiries of the Ministry retained and a man with 25 or 30 years' service released to make his retention possible.
Our system for deciding which employees are to be laid off when a reduction in force has to be implemented represents a sound compromise between a number of conflicting points of view, and it ensures that the interests and rights of veterans are given proper consideration. The lay-off of employees at Point Edward naval base, like all lay-offs, is a matter for deep regret, but those affected by it, both veterans and non-veterans, were treated in accordance with the rules that have been established to ensure that equity and justice prevail when civilians have to be laid off by the department.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I realize that in rising to speak on this serious subject of unemployment, referred to in the speech from the throne once as the recurring problem of seasonal unemployment, I am braving the displeasure of the Prime Minister, who referred to our intervention Tuesday as obstruction. Indeed, this debate on this major problem has been designated in some quarters as a filibuster. If it is a filibuster, Mr. Chairman, it is very strange indeed that 19 supporters of the government, not including the minister's intervention the other evening, have participated in it.
The fact is that this discussion has been prolonged, of course, because of the serious nature of the problem and our inability to secure from the government the information
Supply-Labour
and the plans which we think the problem requires. While the House of Commons is the place for a debate of this kind, I feel, and I think most members will agree with me, that a more appropriate mechanism, if you like, for analysis and examination of the problem, with suggestions to be made, with experts and officials to be called as witnesses, would have been a committee of this house. However, this has not been made possible by the government, so we discuss the matter in committee of the whole.
I do not feel that the government has done justice to this situation in the statements that have been made by only one minister, the Minister of Labour, who of course is the one primarily concerned. I do not believe the minister himself has taken this committee into his confidence as he should have done. He has not even informed us of the steps, however inadequate they may be, that the government has taken.
We had proof of that, Mr. Chairman, only this afternoon as the result of a question addressed by the hon. member for Gloucester. We know from the reply to that question, and we know from reading the newspapers from Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, that in those provinces a joint federal-provincial economic study and analysis of the unemployment problem is to begin shortly.
Here was a step which might have been of some importance in dealing with this matter in that part of Canada. Here was a matter which we had brought up ourselves in this debate, and we had asked for information concerning it. We got that information through the speech from the throne in the legislature of Nova Scotia and through the newspapers of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. I say with all respect to the minister that I think he owed it to this committee to give us that information at the beginning of this debate.
We on this side do not underestimate the difficulties of the problems of employment and unemployment with which the government is confronted. We know, as well as the minister, that this is a tragic human problem for all those who wish to work and cannot find work. We learned this afternoon of the increasing number of people in that unhappy category. We know also that this problem has to be faced and dealt with by the government within the limits imposed on the government by a free society which means, of course, limitation on government authority. It means, of course, that we do not want to order people around, even in the interests of employment.
The very complexity and the very difficulty of this problem and its human importance surely underline the obligation of any government on any level-indeed on all levels-

Supply-Labour
to take every step possible to meet it. As the minister knows, that is why co-operation among all levels of government is essential if this problem is going to be dealt with effectively.
Furthermore, as has been pointed out on this side, not only did this matter require co-operative action by all levels of government but it is too difficult, too fundamental, too all-embracing a problem and too complex for any one department of any government, including the federal government. As has already been suggested on this side, it should be taken over by the government as a whole, and there should be set up some kind of central planning agency along the lines, as a matter of fact, that this party has put forward more than once during the last three years, going back to the election of 1958, by the establishment of a committee on development, employment and automation about which I hope to have a few words to say later.
When we suggest that perhaps this problem is beyond the scope and the authority of any single department of government, of course that is no reflection on the Department of Labour and certainly no reflection on the minister. It is our view that the present mechanism for dealing with what is becoming a continuing problem in this country is just not good enough.
Let me give you one example, Mr. Chairman, in respect of a new development or a new form in which this problem has arisen. Let us take as an example the uranium areas of Bancroft, Uranium City and Elliot Lake. They are areas of new development, of resource exploitation where we are now facing, or indeed where we now have a surplus employment area almost before the development has been completed; I refer to the physical development. This experience-and it is not a happy one- is not going to be unique in this country. In the future other areas will develop, grow up and find themselves in that situation. The old days when the worker could fold his tent when a mine was exhausted and silently steal away into the night are gone, and they are not likely to return in our complex industrial civilization. Furthermore, the workers today will not tolerate that kind of industrial development. Pioneering of that sort is finished.
That means, among other things, that government must give more consideration than has been given in the past-and I am not talking only about the last three winters -to this kind of development and the situation regarding employment in those areas when they face conditions which they perhaps did not expect when the development began. This means that governments, provincial and federal, in this country will be obliged to

plan ahead in order to meet this situation in a way in which it has not been done in the past.
If, for instance, this government knew that this situation was going to develop in these three areas-and it now claims that it did; indeed, it reproaches us on this side for not having been aware of it five years ago. The government now claims it knew this situation was going to develop, although I must say that the words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce in this house last summer and the year before do not seem to be very convincing evidence of that fact. But if the government did know that this situation was developing, what was done to prepare for the resulting unemployment which, in the light of that fact, was inevitable? That is a problem, and we are going to have that problem repeated in this country in the years ahead.
Then there is another problem; or rather it is another aspect of the same problem of unemployment. There is the problem of the redevelopment of old established areas now slowly declining. There are in Canada areas that are faced with this social and economic unemployment problem. We therefore ask ourselves this question, and the government should be asking itself the same question. Are we going to have in this new, vigorous, buoyant and undeveloped country depressed areas with a steady and high level of unemployment? Are we going to have as endemic, as imbedded in the structure of this country, the kind of situation that is referred to in the editorial in the Halifax Chronical-Herald of February 24?
I might just read a couple of paragraphs from that editorial. It refers to the situation in Pictou county in Nova Scotia. The editorial states:
What is required, and required immediately, is a recognition by federal and provincial authorities that a serious social and economic crisis has developed in Pictou county and that extraordinary treatment must be applied to overcome it.
And again:
A few weeks ago we calculated in these columns, on the basis of information obtained from the national employment service, that one half of the industrial force of Pictou county was idle. This desperate plight is steadily getting worse.
The editorial goes on to state as follows:
The appeals that have gone out from labour, religious and other groups for federal measures to alleviate this regional poverty in the midst of what Ottawa claims to be national prosperity have drawn no more than officialdom's stereotyped niceties in reply.
The last paragraph states as follows:
There must be many in Pictou county crying out in their hearts to Ottawa these days, as the psalmist cried out to his Lord: "How long wilt

thou forget me!" Particularly when they read of how countries of Europe have been successfully restoring the economies of their declining regions with governmental measures.
In that connection it is interesting to see what has been done in the United Kingdom to convert depressed areas into areas of new industrial development. It is worthy of study, especially in its application to the problems we face. It is the kind of study which undoubtedly would be made by the committee of which I have spoken. Indeed, perhaps such a study, although I do not know, is being made by the Department of Labour. We can certainly learn a great deal from United Kingdom experience in facing this kind of problem.
So we ask ourselves the question. Can we in this country work out arrangements, national and regional, to anticipate this kind of difficulty? The minister now tells us that he is beginning the process of working out such an arrangement with Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. Of course we wish him well in this activity, even though we are, to say the least, surprised that we had not heard about it at the beginning of this debate.

There is no division of opinion, surely, on the seriousness of the problem we face, even though we may have different opinions about its nature. Even if we disagree, Mr. Chairman, about the figures and the statistics-and perhaps it would be a good thing if we had a truce in the battle of statistics-one of the things we might have been able to do if we had a committee to study unemployment at the present time is to work out a system of measuring the employment and unemployment situation which would have been agreeable to all concerned. If we could have summoned before the committee those in the bureau of statistics and the Department of Labour who work out these figures, and then found out the basis on which they made their calculations, perhaps we would have agreed on an acceptable measuring rod which would have been, I am sure the minister will agree, a very happy result indeed.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING HARM- FUL EFFECT OF POLLUTION ON SEA BIRDS
speechtext: That is right.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING HARM- FUL EFFECT OF POLLUTION ON SEA BIRDS
speechtext:
However, we do agree surely that the problem is serious, and we must admit and accept the fact that it has been serious now for three years, with its impact approaching what are surely tragic proportions in some areas of this country, as the percentage figures which have been tabled in this house indicate beyond possible shadow of doubt, especially in the Atlantic provinces.
Mr. Chairman, the unevenness of the impact of this problem creates its own problems, because it means that measures which are taken uniformly on a national basis are uneven in their benefits to various parts of the country. There is no better example of that than the winter works program. The winter works program is fine to the extent that it gives work which would not have otherwise been available; but it is inadequate, surely, in the face of the problem before us. It has not been planned sufficiently in advance either this year or last year, and it undoubtedly is uneven in its results.
As has been pointed out in this debate, and it is a very important point with which I hope the minister will deal, the richest communities and municipalities in this country where unemployment in some cases is least, and which are in the best position and the easiest position to deal with the problem, are those which are benefiting most by this

Supply-Labour
winter works program. And some of the areas which are suffering most, by their very poverty are getting the least from the program because they are not able to meet conditions which have been laid down.
How many men have been put to work by this program? I think the minister said that he hoped there would be 40,000 this year for an indeterminate period of time, and I think last year it was 32,000 or 34,000; something like that. But I ask the minister how many of those 40,000 or 34,000 would have been working on these projects even if there had been no federal help. We do not know, perhaps; but we do know that some of the municipalities, at least, especially the ones which have come into this program, are those which are the richest and strongest, so some of them would have gone ahead with the program without help. Therefore employment which is included in the 40,000 figure would have been provided in any event.
Then the minister and hon. members opposite made comparisons with the late thirties. It was said that things were just as bad or worse then. Well, Mr. Chairman, we on this side have not accepted the validity of that comparison or the validity of all the statistics used, but surely no one can get any comfort from the comparison even if it is accepted on the terms on which it was put forward to us by the government. In the thirties we had a terrible depression. Now we are told we are not in the midst even of a recession. We are told the recession is over, even though the jobless are still with us. So, Mr. Chairman, what comfort can one get from a comparison, regardless of the basis on which it is made, between the situation now and the situation in the thirties?
The seriousness of the problem, then, is obvious, but the nature of the problem I suggest is not understood. And it is not easy to understand, because there are different kinds of unemployment. And the differentiation between them is becoming clearer each year we are faced with this problem. When the speech from the throne talked only about recurrent seasonal unemployment it gave the impression that this is the only kind of unemployment which causes this problem in this country at this time. As a matter of fact there are three quite distinct kinds of unemployment, and unless we keep the distinction between them clear in our minds it will be hard to do very much about them.
The first, of course, is the cyclical or if you like economic unemployment due to the ups and downs of the business cycle, it is not only a problem requiring national solutions, if it can be solved at all, but also to international action.
Then there is the problem of technological, sometimes called structural, unemployment where people lose their jobs not through the changes in the business cycle so much as through changes in technology, changes in consumer preference-the textile industry is a good example of that-the lack or depletion of resources or the development of geographical disadvantages. All that kind of thing makes this sort of unemployment something quite different from what I have called cyclical unemployment, and often in contrast to that type of unemployment because it is localized in its effects both in respect of areas and in respect of industries.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING HARM- FUL EFFECT OF POLLUTION ON SEA BIRDS
speechtext: Could I ask a question purely for my own understanding, Mr. Chairman. When the hon. member uses the word "cyclical" he does not mean the same as "seasonal", does he?

subsubtopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING HARM- FUL EFFECT OF POLLUTION ON SEA BIRDS
speechtext:
No, Mr. Chairman, I do not, and I am glad my hon. friend pointed out the possibility of that kind of misunderstanding. By cyclical unemployment I mean unemployment caused by the rise and fall of the business cycle not only in our country but internationally and it is something, as I have said, that we can do something about nationally but cannot cure by national action alone. The problem requires international co-operation, and I will be talking about that matter when we get on to trade questions.
In addition to the cyclical and the technological unemployment we have the kind of unemployment which is most in our minds in this country, and because it is so much in our minds it confuses the issue at times and makes it more difficult for government to deal with the whole problem. I refer, of course, to what the government itself has called in the speech from the throne-the only kind of unemployment which was mentioned-seasonal unemployment. That is, of course, unemployment which is brought about by variations in climate, with which we will always be faced in this country. If not for always at least for some time we cannot overcome completely the effects of climate. So we have to keep these three types of unemployment distinct in our minds if we are to find any solution to the problem.
The cyclical, the first kind of unemployment, I suspect is not very high in this country at the present time because the low point in the business cycle, we have been told by experts of the government, was passed in 1958 and a recovery has been going on since the summer of that year. We have also been told that at this particular time, March 1960, we are at the crest of the cycle. In that sense 1960 may be a comparable year to 1956, which was at the crest of the

business cycle of that era. Yet, Mr. Chairman, that makes one feel all the more worried about the situation which faces us; because if when at the crest of this cycle, in a year of expansion and prosperity which we are told we are going to have-and we have had a report today from the Minister of Trade and Commerce which indicated that investment intentions were going up 4.6 per cent next year-if in the middle of that kind of situation we have this amount of unemployment, which is far from normal, what will be the effect on the employment situation in this country when we get over that crest and approach the other side of the cyclical curve? We all hope without exception in this committee that these economists and experts who are now predicting that the recession phase of the cycle will soon be upon us are wrong, but in any event whether they are right or wrong the current unemployment situation cannot be explained in cyclical terms without creating more anxiety than comfort.
As for the seasonal unemployment problem, no one knows precisely what proportion of our unemployed are without jobs because of seasonal factors. I have seen a figure which suggests that perhaps 50 per cent of the unemployment is due to that factor. But whatever the figure may be it is a very serious part of the problem the exact nature of which I suspect we do not yet fully understand.
What are we doing about it? We talk about the winter works program but we all know that that is having a limited effect, indeed what we hope to gain by the winter works program in terms of employment will be more than neutralized by the amount of employment we are going to lose by the reduction in construction and housing in this country.
The dominion bureau of statistics issued a report a little while ago to the effect that more than one third of the decline in jobs in January of this year compared with the end of December 1959 was due to the drop in construction. The figure given, I think, was a drop of 50,000 jobs. That drop will more than neutralize the 40,000 jobs which we hope our winter works program will provide. We learned today from the white paper we had tabled this afternoon and at which I have had a chance only to have a brief glance that investment intentions for 1960 in the field of construction and housing are going to be down from the past year.
What can we do about this seasonal problem? The first thing, surely, is to learn more about it. We should learn more about a problem that is now regular and persistent 79951-0-107}
Supply-Labour
and has gone on long enough in this country to lend itself to the diagnosis which is, I am told, the first step before a cure.
We should learn why this problem varies from one region to another both in its timing, in its magnitude and in its nature. I have been told that there are studies of this matter going on in the Department of Labour. I certainly hope so, but if that is the case they certainly have not been made public. Perhaps they are not as complete as I believe desirable and as might happen if there were a special employment committee charged with the responsibility of analysis and report and the recommendations of solutions.
That is why we reiterate that in facing this No. 1 domestic problem the best brains of government on all levels, of business and of the universities should be brought together to make an analysis-especially a regional analysis-as necessary to ensure proper action. As we have already pointed out, in any study of that kind an important part would have to be played by the representatives of the trade unions and perhaps also of agriculture. That, I suggest, would be the first step.
The second step, surely, would have to be -and this has already been mentioned-a conference with the provinces and municipalities on this question of seasonal unemployment. The responsibility in this matter is not exclusively that of the federal government. It is a joint responsibility and the problem will be solved only as a result of co-ordinated attack on all levels of government on the problem itself. We will have to work out in this country a far more comprehensive program in this attack than that which is embodied in the winter works program which is before us at the present time. It is the kind of problem that will have to be kept under continuous survey by some permanent government agency. It may be unrealistic to think it can be completely eliminated in a climate like ours but it can surely be greatly reduced.
There is the third kind of unemployment, the technological. What can we do about that? It is responsible, I suppose, for a very high proportion of the unemployment we have had over the years. The adjustments today which are required by technological advances which we cannot stop and should not try to stop and the steps to meet these technological changes are difficult, but if they are not taken technological unemployment will become a permanent or perhaps a semi-permanent part of our economic and social fabric.
I ask the government what it has done to meet this problem or to show its awareness

Supply-Labour
of it? Perhaps I can mention particularly one aspect of it which is very much in everybody's mind and which particularly commands the attention of trade unions, and that is the problem of automation.
The Minister of Labour said the other night that he had had nothing from us. My friend the hon. member for Laurier certainly mentioned some proposals the other day, three or four of which I should like to repeat because they have a direct bearing on this problem. One is the expansion of the vocational training program. A second, which was put forward by us as far back as three winters ago, is the establishment of a special capital fund to encourage industrial development in the Atlantic provinces. Another is the establishment of a national advisory board on economic development, automation and employment to which I have already referred. Another is the establishment of a national science commission to promote, sponsor and co-ordinate scientific research and development to ensure a more effective use of our resources, as put forward by us in 1958.
I have attempted to state the problem, Mr. Chairman. It is not going to be solved by just assuming that the laws of nature and of economics will take care of these things and that eventually everything will be fine again and people will go back to work. The recession is over, we are told, and they have not gone back to work.
At the time, when we are worried about this unemployment problem and wondering what steps the government can take to put people back to work by accelerating expansion in our economy, the governor of the Bank of Canada and the Minister of Finance-particularly the governor of the Bank of Canada -tells us that we are living beyond our means and so we have to cut down on unnecessary capital expenditures.
What happens if we are going to do that? There are some signs in government financial policy now which indicate that that is going to be done. Are we going to have more unemployment because of the necessities of fiscal and monetary policy?
Let me refer to what the Minister of Finance said as far back as January 21, 1958, as reported at page 3569 of Hansard:
Let me make it abundantly clear to every member of the house-that the instructions that have been given by the government are to the effect that while we are seeking to reduce expenditure where expenditure is needless we have said that there shall be no reduction in expenditure where it means Jobs, and we are seeking to increase construction in useful public works down the line.
That statement was made by the minister at that time but if we look at the situation today in regard to government intention

with regard to expenditures we find in the current estimates before us under the standard objects, in object No. 13 which deals with the construction or acquisition of plant or works-and that is the estimate which should mean most in terms of employment-the amount in the main estimates for 1959-60 is $430,759,973 but the amount this year is $357,409,179, or a drop of $73,350,794; in that phase of expenditure which is designed, so the Minister of Finance told us two years ago, to create the jobs which he sought to have created irrespective of fiscal considerations.
So we are bound to ask ourselves the question-and with a great deal of anxiety-if we have this present unemployment with our present activity, what will happen if we allow, or even attempt to direct, a slow-down of that activity for anti-inflationary or balance-of-payments reasons? I am not suggesting we do that. There is a good deal of argument-and it will be a long drawn out economic and financial argument-that will be going on in the next two or three months on this point.
But what will be the effect of such a policy on unemployment if it is instituted? In other words, how can we have stability, financial stability, without more unemployment in a free society? How can we check unwise expansion without checking full employment? Every government in our democratic society that I know anything about today, including our own, is committed to the proposition of full employment, and rightly so. How can we have that and at the same time check inflationary dangers? How can we slow down an unhealthy boom in some areas of our country, or of our economy, without making bad conditions even worse in other areas? If development should slow down, or even is slowed down deliberately, it may check inflationary dangers but it may also have the result of bringing about-and I quote from Mr. Coyne's speech in Winnipeg, which I am sure most hon. members have read-it may also have the effect of bringing about those "fluctuations in the level of employment", which, as the governor of the bank points out, by themselves may cause inflation.
Surely, Mr. Chairman, this points up something that perhaps we are at times apt to forget. The importance of spending in an economy such as ours, in a situation such as that in which we find ourselves today, is not so much in the amount spent, but in the nature of the spending and in the area of the spending. Perhaps all levels of governments should be more selective in spending instead of trying to cut down right

across the board. For instance, we hear a great deal of talk these days-we have had a lot of it in the house-about the value of the government's housing program in the creation of employment, a program which is being cut down. While we hear this talk in the House of Commons the governor of the Bank of Canada, a man with some influence in these matters, points out that there is a danger in this kind of spending, and I quote from his speech in Winnipeg, where he says:
It is evident also that through pursuing an excessive rate of growth a quantity of business investment in new enterprises or for expansion has been undertaken in too much of a hurry, at high cost, in directions which perhaps should not have been exploited at all, or not until the following year or later years.
Then, he goes on:
Clearly, not all capital spending contributes to sound growth, or to any growth.
He suggests it does not even contribute to sound employment policy on all occasions. How, then, is a democratic government in a federal state going to control the direction as well as the amount of spending and investment to ensure that it does have maximum social, economic and employment benefits, without running into those other dangers that the governor of the Bank of Canada talks about, or without taking much more control of the economy than in the case at present or that public opinion would permit government to take at present?
Mr. Coyne said that if we had been wise in recent years we might have built fewer houses, and I quote from his speech:
We would have had somewhat less in the way of natural resource development. . . and would of course have had somewhat less spending on public buildings and other public facilities.
He then warned us that even the expansion of the kind that we had in this country out of which we all took so much pride and from which we get our vision of the future was not, and I quote from his speech:
contributing to the maintenance of stable employment conditions.
He goes on to say that other countries where expansion has been more moderate have had as good a record, or a better record of employment than Canada. Therefore, I ask again, can we have full employment, full freedom of enterprise, a minimum of government interference and an expanding economy all at the same time? How are we going to balance one against the other, if we cannot have them all at the same time?
These, Mr. Chairman, are the problems and short of international peace and security there are no more important problems facing the government.
Supply-Labour
Are these situations that I have talked about, which cause so much anxiety, to become built-in, a part of our democratic and federal economic structure? This would be intolerable. The day has gone by when the people would accept it for long. So what is the remedy? I am not in a position to put forward a concrete proposal which immediately would put 200,000 or 300,000 people to work. It cannot be done that way in working out government policy. Even if I were the government I could not do it that way, and in any event I have not that responsibility at the present time. That rests over there. I have some understanding, I hope, of their difficulties, and perhaps it is not possible to put forward this kind of exciting proposal which will have that result immediately. But, as I have tried to suggest in this statement, the first thing to be done to find a remedy is a far-reaching, full-scale examination of the problem, not only in its emeigency aspects in relation to the present situation, but in its long term aspects as a developing and dangerous part of our society; this built-in unemployment that we face. '
There is something else we have to accept. The wealthier parts of this country will have to accept obligations, perhaps in the way they have not in the past, to the economically weaker and less developed parts of the country and to help value their special problems. There is only one way it can be done. And it has been done in the United Kingdom. If you read the United Kingdom program for the depressed areas you will see how it was done. Nor did they have the financial and economic resources over there at that time that we have in this country now. The only way it can be done is by government schemes of capital assistance to encourage industrial and economic re-development in those areas. Perhaps this re-development aspect of the problem is as important as new development projects in our economy. If that should mean-and I suppose it would-heavier tax burdens, no Canadian has the right to complain if the taxes, if the money from those taxes, is used to put into effect constructive and forwardlooking plans worked out in co-operation with the provinces so that we will not have underdeveloped areas in this country indefinitely in the future. I am thinking, of course, particularly, of the Atlantic provinces.
We have had this problem with us now too long for superficial and temporary measures which are mere panaceas. Therefore I express the hope that the government will soon be able to come up with something much better than this winter works program. If they do, and if we put into effect sensible

Supply-Labour
taxation, trade, fiscal and investment policies, and if we get the co-operation of all levels of government, we in the federal parliament can, I think, go far to overcome those employment difficulties in so far as any government can overcome them at all. There are things governments cannot do, and there are things that domestic policy cannot accomplish because international action can spoil all our best plans.
If we do not take this approach we will probably be faced with a worse situation next year. We will be debating this matter all over again next year and perhaps even for a longer period of time than we are doing now. We will have it all over again next session. So surely the government would be well advised to give this possibility, this danger, this dilemma the most serious, expert and urgent consideration and then take the necessary action to deal with it in the light of that consideration.
Chronic unemployment is the problem. It is serious and it is increasing. It is not going to be resolved merely by a change in the economic climate or by the maintenance of what we call normal prosperity. Surely we have learned that over the last three years. There is something new about this problem in the last few years. There is something more worrying about it. This hard core of unemployment is building up and accumulating. It is now becoming a menacing long term problem and if we should face another recession with the chronic unemployment of this present period remaining high then we would be in very serious trouble indeed.

Mr. Chairman, I feel this is one of the most important debates that has

taken place in the House of Commons in recent years. I think that statement is borne out by the fact that members of all parties in the house, over a period now running into the eighth day, have taken part in this important debate. Some years ago when the country was in the depths of a great depression it was the unanimous belief that parliament and the country must do everything possible to maintain full employment. That belief was prevalent during the war. That belief was prevalent at the federal-provincial conference held in 1945 and in the green book proposals that were put forward at that time.
Economists of the day said that steps were necessary in order to provide full employment and full employment was defined as a condition where there were not more than two per cent of the working force out of work at one time. When members of the C.C.F. stated in the past that in our opinion full employment could not be provided without a very fundamental change in the economic system, without bringing in a system of social and economic planning, we were sneered at. We were told that our statements implied blue ruin and that if we would merely let the economic system take its head then, with either the Liberal or the Conservative party in power, we would have full employment. That belief has not been borne out by the facts.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING HARM- FUL EFFECT OF POLLUTION ON SEA BIRDS

subsubtopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING HARM- FUL EFFECT OF POLLUTION ON SEA BIRDS

speechtext:
A further disturbing feature that seems to have crept into our discussion is the apparent acceptance by the government of the situation as being a normal one. The item in the estimates before the house today is an important one. It is an item that is necessary but it is an item of only $15 million. It is an item that, without question, provides for some additional projects and some additional employment in the country at this time. But the item in the estimates is not only inadequate to meet the grave unemployment situation, with over 800,000 unplaced applicants, but it is also inadequate precisely because such a small proportion of the total cost of projects is provided by the item. An estimate has been made that only 13 or 14 per cent of the cost of projects is provided for through the payment of labour under this item.
The Minister of Labour has taken part in the debate formally and informally. He has taken part in the debate at times by making rather lengthy statements and at other times he has merely entered the debate to ask questions or, for a very short period, to hurl accusations at the opposition. However, the minister said one thing for which I give him full marks. He said that the government has taken the responsibility and recognizes the responsibility. The government has taken the responsibility and recognizes the responsibility but it is not prepared to deal with the question, nor is it prepared to act in a forthright manner.
The thing that disturbs me is the apparent evidence that the government does not consider the problem nearly as important as it did two years ago. While the government considered the question of unemployment as important shortly after taking office and was prepared at that tme to undertake certain measures to deal with the problem, today there is a growing body of evidence to support the contention that the government not only is not concerned about unemployment but is taking action that will make unemployment even more serious and drastic than it was a few years ago.
The minister, in speaking in this house on February 24 said, as recorded at page 1404 of Hansard, that after this government took
Supply-Labour
office in 1957 they had undertaken certain actions to deal with the unemployment situation. I quote:
Housing was stimulated.
Then, he says:
Public works were stepped up in order to help those who might find themselves without employment. Then we extended the unemployment insurance benefits by an additional two months in the seasonal class.
He went on to say that deficit budgeting was brought about in order to stimulate employment. Those were real actions that were taken at that time and, no doubt, they resulted in substantial numbers of people being placed in jobs who would not have been so placed if the government had not taken these actions. But the government, as I see it, has been facing two main problems. They have been facing the problem of inflation and the problem of unemployment. I think there is some contest within the cabinet as to how the government should deal with the question of inflation and the question of unemployment. The Minister of Finance has taken a rather cynical attitude, namely that he is going to do, within the terms of the free enterprise outlook, everything he can to balance the budget no matter what the results might be.
I think it is the Minister of Finance who is determining economic policy for this government today. The economic policy of this government is to hold down expenditures, to hold down even some of those expenditures that undoubtedly would result in further employment in this country. 1 have in my hand the main estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1961 and they show the estimates of the Department of Public Works for public buildings, construction and services. The Minister of Labour, in saying how the government dealt with this question in 1957, made it as an important point that public works were stepped up in order to help those who might find themselves without employment. However, the estimates for the coming year show the government has reversed its position. The estimates as tabled show that the Department of Public Works will spend $16.5 million less for the construction of public buildings in the current fiscal year. This is not the way to deal with the unemployment problem, either the unemployment problem that is with us today or the unemployment problem that, unfortunately, will be with us 12 months from now if the government does not take action different from that which it is now taking.
The minister made a great thing about the government extending unemployment insurance. That was done. However, after the

Supply-Labour
government had extended unemployment insurance certain action was taken to make it more difficult tor the workers to get unemployment insurance. I refer to the very controversial, and I think discriminatory, regulations Nos. 172 and 173 which in certain instances deny unemployment insurance benefits to the workers of this country. For the first time, accrued holiday pay is classified as income to prevent workers from receiving unemployment insurance benefits. Severance pay is placed in this same category, and this is another cause for dissatisfaction amongst the unemployed at Elliot Lake. Although these people have received the very small sum of $400 for severance pay, that $400 is melting now when they are without work. The unemployment insurance commission, without even referring this to the unemployment insurance advisory committee, have initiated these regulations which, in my opinion, are discriminatory and deprive unemployed people of the benefits to which they are rightly entitled.
I have in mind the minister's own statement that action was taken so far as the unemployment insurance commission is concerned, and in addition that action will be taken soon, apparently, to rescind these vicious regulations to which I have referred. I am informed that the unemployment insurance advisory committee is meeting tomorrow and I hope, as a result of their representations, this very necessary action will be taken.
The minister has said that on previous occasions the government decided that housing should be stimulated; that the building of houses was an important way to provide jobs in this country. Now we find housing is not being stimulated. As a matter of fact, housing is being slowed down and there have been very few housing starts since January. The Minister of Finance has apparently decreed that money shall be saved if it is possible, so there is no allotment for house construction and this undoubtedly will make the unemployment problem worse than it has been.
The government took office in 1957 and, in the words of the minister, they recognized the unemployment problem existed. They took action. Housing starts ran up in 1958 to 164,632; in 1959 they had dropped to approximately 137,000 and by 1960 they will have dropped down to about 125,000. I am wondering whether even this very low figure will be reached because of the very bad beginning we had in January. Private loans under the act dropped to 100 in January compared with 1,028 for the same month a year earlier and 183 in December. Housing starts also dropped but not as sharply as the loans. They totalled 3,724 across the

country compared with 4,833 in January, 1959 and 7,003 last December. There were 7,000 in January 1958; 4,800 in January, 1959, and down to 3,700 in January this year. So the government record in the field of housing is a bad one.
In recent months housing starts are showing further deterioration. How can the minister claim the government is accepting responsibility for unemployment when the record shows that action by the government will undoubtedly reduce further the employment in this country. The Minister of Finance has decreed that there shall be retrenchment; that there shall be fewer housing starts; that there shall be less money spent on public works. Under the former administration we heard a great deal about an all-powerful minister of trade and commerce. It was alleged that C. D. Howe had great control of the Liberal cabinet. I think C. D. Howe was a pygmy compared with the Minister of Finance in the power that the Minister of Finance is wielding today.
The Minister of Finance says: there will be retrenchment, we will hold down the wages of civil servants; we will cutback housing construction, we will reduce expenditures on public works, no matter what the Minister of Labour may say. The Minister of Labour obviously has little influence on his colleagues who have pulled the rug from under him and have left him with a token estimate of $15 million that does little to deal with the great unemployment emergency facing the country at this time.
We feel the time has come for decided action by the government and we think that action should be taken along a number of lines. I have already suggested this afternoon that regulations 172 and 173 under the Unemployment Insurance Act should be immediately rescinded in order that unemployed persons can have the money to which I believe they are entitled.
This group has already said-and I put this suggestion forward again-that there should be established in this country a national industrial planning board to provide and to stimulate secondary industries in the areas of this country that are depressed. Unemployment across this country is not even. As so frequently happens, the maritimes are experiencing chronic unemployment. There is chronic unemployment in other areas across the country. I do not suppose it will ever be possible in Canada completely to wipe out areas of unemployment and areas in which industries are not able to compete. However, I believe that, as a general principle the people living in large sections of Canada have the right to share in the general wellbeing of the country year in and year out. I

think the maritimes have a legitimate complaint that their areas have been deprived of the right to share in the production of this country.
I put forward as the third proposition the the suggestion that the government should establish a national manpower board to look after and to promote the retraining of unemployed people, to make provision for their employment in industries and in areas where job opportunities are available and generally to make every recommendation possible to provide full employment in our nation.
The question to which the Minister of Finance has addressed himself, namely the matter of inflation, is an important one. I remember that last session the Prime Minister asked us on this side of the house this question: which is more important, unemployment or stable prices? The government obviously has decided that here are two difficult problems, that it cannot cope with both and that it will make an effort to prevent inflation. I think the government is failing on both counts because prices are continuing to rise and unemployment stays with us. But I think there is action the government should take in the field of prices in this country.
No matter what may be said to the contrary, I believe the Canadian nation is prepared at this time to support government action to prevent prices from rising and going through the ceiling. Some of the main labour organizations in this country, as well as farm organizations and others, have impressed upon the government the need to take action to prevent this continual spiral of inflation.
I am suggesting that at least in key industries there should be established in this country a prices regulation tribunal to which key industries would be obliged to refer before they have the authority or the right to increase their prices. I think particularly of a key industry like the steel industry. I do not think the government should be prepared to allow the steel industry to increase prices at will without first having to substantiate the need for any increase in prices. I think also of the manufacturers of automobiles, as is suggested, or the manufacturers of other key commodities.
I think the people of this country will support action to prevent a continuation of inflation. I agree that if we are going to solve the unemployment problem we must at the same time solve the question of inflation. You cannot plan on one economic front without planning on other economic fronts. That is the dilemma the government is in. The Minister of Finance is in control; he has his own way. The Minister of Labour is a very small
Supply-Labour
and, I am exceedingly sorry to say, ineffective voice apparently in the cabinet; because I am sure he would like greater action from his government in order to deal with the unemployment situation.
I think there is need in this country at this time to increase the income of low income groups, to increase the purchasing power of people with small incomes, of workers who are out of work or low paid workers in depressed areas in this country and people who are engaged in industries and in occupations where income is low.
As the final proposal I would suggest that the government should take action to reduce interest rates in this country which, 1 submit, are preventing the economic expansion required to provide full employment. The position in which we apparently are today is that every party in this chamber wants full employment. The opposition members,, both of the Liberal party and of the C.C.F. party, have offered to the government suggestions and proposals. The Minister of Labour has not heard those proposals. He has refused to say that such proposals have been made. But the government is responsible. It is the job of the government to govern the country, not the job of the opposition. In my opinion, we have discharged our responsibility by bringing forward the problems and by asking the government to consider certain action; but it is the responsibility of the government to take action.
The Prime Minister is committed to full employment. No person in this country has taken a stronger stand in favour of full employment than has the Prime Minister. Reference has been made in this chamber previously-I do not need to refer to it again; it has been quoted often-to the statement of the Prime Minister that as long as he was Prime Minister, everything would be done, without regard to limit, to see that no one suffered from unemployment. According to the last estimate, half a million Canadians are out of work and are looking for jobs. The Prime Minister says no one will suffer from unemployment. The Minister of Labour says: We are unable to deal with this situation; will the opposition give us some ideas? According to the Leader-Post of February 25, 1958, speaking at Cornwall, Ontario the Prime Minister made this statement:
As long as I am prime minister, no person in this country is going to suffer because of unemployment. My heart goes out to those in that position. I've kept my promises in the past. That promise will be kept to the letter.
I ask the Minister of Labour why the Prime-Minister and the government have failed to keep this promise and commitment to the-

Supply-Labour
Canadian people. In the light of the government's commitments to the Canadian people, I suggest to the government that they must take far greater action now than anything that has been contemplated by the government to date. I wish the Minister of Labour well, but I hope that when he speaks he will recognize that something has to be done, that something needs to be done, and that he will have a greater influence amongst his colleagues in the future than he apparently has had in the recent year.
This debate is important. For the life of me I do not know why other cabinet ministers have not taken part in this debate. I do *not know, for example, why the Minister of Public Works has not defined the program *of his department to deal with unemployment. I do not know why the Minister of Trade and Commerce has not taken part in this debate to show how the policies of his department will increase trade and increase employment opportunities. The Minister of Finance has not graced us with his presence in this debate except perhaps on very rare occasions. I will not say cabinet attendance is inadequate at this moment, but it has been inadequate during many parts of this debate.
It is lamentable that on one occasion there was not a single cabinet minister in the chamber when, let me say to the Minister of Labour right now, the Minister of Labour was at the back of the chamber taking a well deserved breather. It is pretty hard for any person to stay in this chamber hour after hour after hour. They are certainly deserving of study on a long range basis, especially the suggestions made this afternoon by the Leader of the Opposition. That study will be given to the recommendations that are found reasonable, but there is nothing revolutionary in any of the suggestions that were made. Many of those things are in effect

now, many are being undertaken in the various departments of government and many will be accelerated as the days go by.
As an example, let me deal with the suggestion made for the calling of a conference on unemployment. These conferences have been called in the past. There was also mention made in this debate of the wisdom of the government announcing the municipal incentive works program at a date earlier than it was announced the year before. We announced it this year by some two months earlier but now hon. members opposite say that was not early enough and that it should be earlier yet. Let me point out, however, that the municipalities have not complained. They felt that this year the announcement was made at a proper time and gave them ample opportunity to prepare for these programs. No complaints of that nature were received from any of the municipalities. We complied with the suggestion made last year and announced the program two months earlier, in the first week of September.
As I said earlier, I do not want to hurt anyone's feelings in this respect, but there is nothing new in most of the suggestions that have been made. As I say, they will be very carefully examined and those that are new, that have merit, that are reasonable suggestions most certainly will be given every consideration and study. We talk about the seasonal problem, and many people are surprised that that problem is still with us. But I say that we are dealing with a problem that has been with us since confederation. The simple fact of the matter is that we have such a climate in this country that at this time of the year, with the kind of weather conditions we have had in the last month, there is a segment of our people which does not work, and naturally so. Many of the construction jobs it this country cannot be carried on when we have such large amounts of snow covering the ground, and most certainly this means that people in the construction industry are, of necessity, laid off.
Because of our weather conditions we have a most unsuitable climate for winter work, and we have a tremendous concentration of primary research development which is subject to seasonal dislocation. In these two facts alone lies the explanation of recurring winter and seasonal unemployment in Canada. All the economists have agreed on this, and there are a number of reports to this effect. They have been making those reports for the last quarter of a century, and they have warned us that this situation is not getting better but worse.
Supply-Labour
The answer is that we must have more secondary industry in this country and everyone knows this. It is beginning to penetrate the minds even of hon. members opposite. We are in a state of transition as a supplier of primary products for secondary processing in the United States. That is where the market area is and that is where the markets are. It is in the secondary processing that you have the high content of skilled labour.
This government is aware of the situation and our policies are being directed toward dealing with the situation. It is a situation which has been getting more pronounced since the war; it is a situation which must be dealt with by encouraging secondary industries, by encouraging processing and manufacturing industries. We are doing this and we will continue to do it. Mind you, Mr. Chairman, it will not be done overnight, but it will be done. We will carry on with the job, as was requested by the Canadian Labour Congress when they presented their brief just a short while ago.
The Leader of the Opposition mentioned the fact that the government claims the recession is over. It is not only the government that claims the recession is over. The Canadian Labour Congress, which is vitally interested in this matter, and which in the past two years severely criticized the government and asked it to do something about it, said in its brief a short while ago, and said very factually, that the recession is over. Bank presidents and other people have said the same thing. The government are not the only people who are saying that this is a fact; other people are saying it. I am very much surprised that the only people I hear expressing contrary points of view on this matter are the opposition in this house. I think it is getting to be fairly obvious that seasonal unemployment in this country is a continuing problem.
I am very much surprised that the opposition should say that we in our two and one-half years in office should eliminate something that has been recurring, and continually recurring, winter after winter, for the past 22 years.

I should like to say a few words on training. A number of suggestions have been made in this regard. I must say, as I have said on a previous occasion, that no one is satisfied with the present state of affairs as far as training is concerned. As Canada moves into secondary industry and as the rate of industrial growth is accelerated, certainly more training will be required. New programs will be worked out and they must of necessity be worked out with the co-operation of the provinces. But in addition I feel that they must and will be worked out with industry and with the unions, keeping in mind the special problems of regional difficulty and of technological changes. We have made a beginning on these things and we will carry them through, I hope, to a successful conclusion. I think that would be good planning and these steps should bring about satisfactory results.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, let me say that the mistakes of many years cannot be rectified in a few months. We have our programs and we have our policies. In the main they are directed to the problem which confronts us. In what the Toronto Star called on February 19 "a period of unprecedented boom" I am sure these problems will continue to exist. However, I want to say that I do not believe they will be overcome by following a depression psychology. They cannot be solved by a deliberate sowing of hysteria or panic. Mr. Chairman, this program of campgrounds and picnic sites was first inaugurated as a method of helping winter employment. The first program of 1957-58 started after Christmas. The effective date was January 2. In that winter of 195758, nine provinces participated, the exception being Quebec. The following year we started the program earlier, on October 30, and seven provinces participated that year. This present winter, 1959-60, the program started at the same time, October 30, and to date eight provinces have accepted the federal offer, and Prince Edward Island has indicated that it is considering participation.
In so far as the money is concerned, in the first year 1957-58-I am now giving fiscal

year figures because the figure covers two fiscal years in each winter

there was nothing in the main estimates, but we put $1 million in the supplementaries that year. The actual expenditures in that year, up to the end of March, were $0.49 million. In the fiscal year 1958-59 the main estimates had a figure of $1 million, and the supplementaries $1.5 million and we actually expended $1.72 million. In the fiscal year 1959-60, the estimates were $1.5 million and the supplementaries were

and it is the supplementary we are dealing with now-$0.8 million. The estimated expenditure for this winter is $2.3 million. The estimates for next year show a figure of $0.8 million, and we estimate from the indications from the provinces we will require in the supplementaries next winter $0.9 million, for a total estimate of $1.7 million.
If you take the same figures of actual expenditures by winters rather than by fiscal years, the first program from January 2, 1958 to March 31, 1958 actually accounted for $1.3 million by the federal government. Therefore, the actual expenditure that winter was $2.6 million, when you take the 50 per cent that the provinces had to provide. In the second winter, from November 1, 1958 to May 31, 1959 the actual expenditures were $1.81 million, or $3.62 million when the combined totals are added up.
The third winter, of course, is an estimate. The estimate at the present time is $1.85 million. This is on the basis of present indications by the provinces. The amount committed to date and authorized by the governor in council under this $1.85 million is $1.25 million, or an actual expenditure to date over the three winters of $3.46 million. Of course, to get the total amount you double that.
In answer to the other question asked by the hon. member about the program itself, I would like to say this. Even though this program was originally started primarily because of our desire to help winter unemployment, actually it was because of a real conviction that it was a good program. The idea originated in the dominion-provincial tourist conference in the fall of 1957, and we took this suggestion as one way to help winter unemployment and at the same time carry out a very useful program for those who travel on our highways.
This year there is no great change in the program except that we have asked the provinces, in fairness to the federal government, to put up a plaque on each of these picnic sites or campgrounds which shows that the site or campground is a co-operative effort by the two governments, and that is all the plaque says.
