The second question dealt with the discussions that took place between the provincial government and ourselves about the possibility of making Garibaldi a national park. At the moment this matter is inactive. The federal government expects certain conditions to be met by a provincial government before a national park is set up. The provincial government must agree that all resources in the proposed national park area will be turned over to the federal government free of encumbrance. This means that all the timber, wild life, mineral and recreational resources of the area can only be used as laid down in the National Parks Act. In other words, you cannot take off timber or move in and take out any minerals that may exist. There are also certain limitations on the types of recreation that may be carried on in a national park compared with a provincial park.
For these reasons I would imagine that the provincial government decided that it would like to look a little longer at how it could make use of Garibaldi park, for it has much greater freedom than we would have in using the resources of the park area.

The thinking now is that sometimes it may be considered against the public interest to set aside areas in the completely natural state that the National Parks Act requires as opposed to the setting up of an area as a recreational area.
If it is a recreational area, we are allowed to use the forests without destroying their beauty; we are allowed to take out the minerals and put something back in their place to keep the area just as beautiful. We are allowed to use all the resources to the best advantage, without setting aside forever the exploitation of the resources of the area. This is one of the limitations we have in the National Parks Act. We keep the National Parks Act going for obvious reasons, because we want to preserve some of our most beautiful areas forever so that future generations can see this country as it was in, the beginning.

I should like to take this opportunity of complimenting the minister for the excellent service that has been given, especially in British Columbia. If I can get the information for which I have asked, I should appreciate it.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
I wonder
whether I might be allowed to answer those two questions before they get too far advanced? The hon. member for St. Denis asked for the amount by which Quebec had benefited. To date it has been nil because they have not entered into the agreement the first winter nor the second winter. I am hopeful that they will reconsider their stand and come in on this program. There have been conversations with one or two of their ministers within the last two or three months and I am hopeful they will be fruitful.
The hon. member asked for the amount of money in each province. The hon. member for Kootenay East asked for the same thing. I can give the committee the figures for the two years which are complete, 1957-1958 and

Supply-Northern Affairs
1958-	1959. For British Columbia, for the first year 1957-58 the figure is $367,000. I will just use the round figures. The next year for British Columbia the figure is $387,000. For Alberta, the first year $104,000, the second year $225,000. For Saskatchewan, the first year $36,000, the second year $122,000. For Manitoba, the first year $90,000, the second year $125,000. For Ontario, the first year $604,000, the second year $880,000. For Nova Scotia, the first year $8,500, the second year $43,000. For Prince Edward Island, the first year $2,000, the second year nil. For Newfoundland, the first year $54,000, the second year nil. I have not the figures for the present winter.

Mr. Chairman, I think I made a mistake when I said that in Quebec we have the best government since confederation; what I should have said was, according to Union Nationale. While I am on my feet I should like to know which of the premiers the minister was in communication with regarding this item, and what amount of money has been spent by the federal government up to date without Quebec having any share of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not think it is proper for me to mention individual names of ministers until some decision has been made. As to the second question, I did give the total figures at the opening of my remarks and I think you will be able to find them on the record tomorrow.
The total amount which has been spent to date by the federal government is $4.36 million. This will be a little larger by the end of the year. The expected amount at the end of the year will be $4.96 million. Roughly $5 million will be our share by the end of the
1959-	60 program. That means the total amount spent in the provinces will be $10 million, because our share is half.

Mr. Chairman, about the communication with the premier of Quebec, how was that done? Was it done by letter or telegram or communication of some kind? Did the minister send the letter or was it the other way round? We are very interested in knowing why Quebec is not sharing in this. We should like to know who is responsible for Quebec not sharing in it.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I sent a letter to the premier of Quebec at the beginning of the program, and a second followup letter was sent to the premier of Quebec but I have forgotten the exact date. There have also been oral conversations in the last two or three months.

Mr. Chairman, I notice in realizing the importance of the minister's remarks that there is nothing constructive as

far as Garibaldi is concerned. This has a rather unique significance. There is the vaguest suspicion in British Columbia that the Conservatives in Ottawa and the Social Credits in British Columbia are one and the same outfit. Now, I hope that is not so.
That is not true.
May I say that this is one time that I hope the expression of opinion of the hon. member for Cariboo is a fact. The minister has as much as admitted-
Pardon me; are you calling me a liar?
Oh, oh.
The Social Credit-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. Will the hon. member please sit down. I heard what the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam said, and I am sure the hon. member for Cariboo is mistaken.

Mr. Chairman, I wish on this occasion to pay my respects to the hon. member who intervened, because I know very well indeed that he is not a supporter of the Social Credit government of British Columbia. He is a Conservative at heart, first, last and always. However, that will not prevent me from entering his riding when I see fit to do so.
However, I regret very much the minister having to admit that none of this money is likely to be spent on Garibaldi. It is important at this time that I raise this issue because of the announcement made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard in respect of the next Olympic games. I admit that he had to be mowed down by the Prime Minister and the Prime Minister had to announce that the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard did not know what he was talking about in regard to the next Olympic games. I feel this is regrettable indeed because here is an opening for Canada to make a name for itself. Here is a chance whereby we might utilize one of our greatest pleasure resorts. However, I feel it will take a little bit of leadership on the part of the minister and he will have to be a spear or a thorn with regard to the decisions made, not only by the existing government of British Columbia but also the governments we have had in the past. Garibaldi has to be made a national park if we are ever going to realize its full potentialities.
I hope that the hon. member for Coast-Capilano is going to participate in this debate because I have read a number of newspaper reports wherein he is reported to have claimed that he is going to fight in order to make a national park out of Garibaldi park. I hope he

will rise in his place and defend the news releases which have been issued either by him or on his behalf in the press.
All I am asking the minister now is, what leadership is the government at this time giving in the direction of making out of Garibaldi park a national park for the purpose that we might be able to share in the vote now before us? This would also provide national park facilities to the majority of the people of British Columbia in the area they now live, that is in the lower mainland.
I ask the minister what leadership his department is giving in that respect or are they humbly submitting to the old attitude of the British Columbia government that someday 100 or 150 years hence they will utilize the minerals in the park but in the meantime will take a dog in the manger attitude and not allow national development?

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word at this time. The area in question is in my riding and is known as Garibaldi park. I should like that understood so that all present will know the area whereof we speak. This is one of the finest alpine beauty spots in the world offering great possibilities for skiing and other sports activities.
I should further like to invite the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam sometime after the session concludes to come to God's country and have a look at the place. I think he might enjoy it. I should also like to extend that invitation to all hon. members of the committee. I can assure them they will receive a hospitable welcome and will see some of Canada's finest scenery.
I wish now to speak about my position in respect to this matter. I observe that the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam is chuckling away to himself, no doubt congratulating himself on having created a great deal of embarrassment for me. I can assure the hon. member that that is not so. I can further assure him that in the past two sessions, and again in this one, also in the areas in my riding, I really do believe, have required no spokesman to represent them other than the man the people of that riding have sent to this House of Commons. In saying this I hope I speak with a certain amount of modesty.
My position is well known on this question. I have announced in my riding and have stated in this chamber that I will support in every way the establishment of a national park in Garibaldi and will urge the federal government to do so when and if the province of British Columbia surrenders that which they now own, the park area. That is my established position and it will be
Supply-Northern Affairs a frosty Friday that the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam or any other succeeds in embarrassing me in relation to the position I have taken because certainly it is well known throughout my area and in my riding.

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. I come from a province that I could talk about at great length too. I would like to know what Olympic games and Garibaldi park have to do with the item we are discussing. I should like to know whether we are all going to spend the evening talking about our own ridings and provinces or devote our attention to the item under consideration.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: As hon. members know I just arrived a few moments ago. I have noticed, however, that some latitude was given. If the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam who has been seeking the floor will assure me that he will speak for only about two minutes I will hear him.

Mr. Chairman, I want to say that I have no intention of putting the hon. member for Coast-Capilano on the spot. I wanted to remind him, though, that Garibaldi park is of as much concern to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam; and the hon. member for Fraser Valley as it is to the hon. member for Coast-Capilano.

Mr. Chairman, I am glad to see that the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River has returned to the committee- at least he was here a moment ago-because I think his criticism of the government's policy in regard to this item was uncalled for and unfair. I am pleased to see the hon. gentleman taking his seat at this moment. If the hon. member had been listening he would have heard the minister say that the amount expended by the government of Canada under this item had increased yearly and that it was not, as he characterized it, an election bait in the election campaign of 1958.
I commend the government for this program. In the province of Alberta we have increased the beauty of our highways under it and I have heard favourable comments from many tourists from all over Canada and the United States.
I should like also to thank the minister for giving us the information he gave tonight concerning the erection of these plaques because in Alberta the provincial government is taking all the credit for the erection of these enjoyable attractions and additions to our highways.

Mr. Chairman, may I just
follow the hon. member for Wetaskiwin to

Supply-Northern Affairs acknowledge that I am in the committee and to say to him that I would go further and state that this is a new policy. I will give full credit to the government for introducing this particular policy but my complaint is that it had not used this policy in the normal, official and proper way. It used this policy, - as I said, in a hanky-panky way for political purposes and not for the relief of unemployment during the winter months.

Mr. Chairman, for several minutes I have been trying to get the Chair's attention to comment on something the minister said a few moments ago. I may be wrong but my memory is that he gave a summary of the total expenditures by provinces during the first two years of the scheme. He mentioned why Quebec was not included but I think he neglected to give any information on the province of New Brunswick. If that was an oversight I would appreciate it if the minister would give the figures, if any, for this province at the present time so the record will be correct.

Mr. Chairman, before we hear from the next hon. member I think the minister should answer the question just put by the hon. member for Westmorland. I can understand why there was no money spent in Quebec but we have in New Brunswick a different government from that in Quebec although I do not always agree with the policies of the government of New Brunswick. Also there are in New Brunswick so many beautiful potential sites for camping grounds and picnic areas that I cannot understand why New Brunswick did not take advantage of this program.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, if I neglected to give the figures for New Brunswick it was purely through inadvertence. The figure for the first year, 1957-58, is $45,000 and for the second year, $27,000.
Could the minister give the figures for Newfoundland?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, for Newfoundland the figure for the first year is $54,000 and for the second year nil.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to say a word or two on this item because it relates to a program in western Canada and particularly in Alberta which I value and under which much benefit has been derived. In Macleod riding which I represent we think a lot of it.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River has said it was hanky-panky and to a certain extent political. The hon. member usually carefully weighs his views before he speaks and I am sure his pronouncements carry much


weight with hon. members of this committee but in this particular instance when he described it as a political program he was completely wrong.
Let us take the province of Alberta for example. This is a co-operative program between the municipalities and the province. The province of Alberta administers the program. The federal government has virtually nothing whatever to say about where the projects are started in a given area or where the camping grounds or picnic areas are developed. Any allusion to the fact that the expenditure of that money is influenced by decision of the federal government is completely erroneous. That is certainly true in my riding and in all the ridings with which I am familiar.
It does not apply to Ontario; it may be right in Alberta.

Let me say this. Allusion was also made by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River to the fact that this item was not exact; in other words, he took issue with the minister and said that more exact figures should be brought before this committee so that we would know exactly the amount that was being spent. Now, he can think twice- and I am sure he is capable of doing this- and he would know that when you are starting these different projects, as these local and provincial governments are doing, you start where the need exists. For instance, in the Crowsnest pass area, during the past month and a half four new campsites and picnic areas were started in order to give employment.
I say, Mr. Chairman, that this program is fitting like a glove into those small areas, giving employment to the people whom one could not reach in any other way. Therefore, I say that those who pick on this program and say it was ill conceived and is being used for political purposes are completely out of order and completly wrong in their statements and such statements deserve to be challenged.
In closing, I want to compliment the minister on this program and I want to compliment the government on what they are doing. If and when there are any additional improvements needed I am sure it will be because of the efforts of those people in the municipalities, those people in the towns, those people in the provinces, who are looking to the dominion to pay 50 per cent of the bill they are putting forward in order to develop ways and means of giving employment and getting useful work done.
I should like the minister to answer this question. How much of the money in this

particular vote is to be devoted to the development of campgrounds, and picnic areas along the main trans-Canada highway? Is the program along the main trans-Canada highway being conducted on a 50-50 basis with the provincial government the same as it is with provincial roads?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: In answer to the hon. member's question, the trans-Canada highway program of campgrounds and picnic sites is a separate vote. The agreement was that over a two-year period there would be an expenditure of $2 million on that item. We will share 50 per cent, but it is not limited to the winter months; it can be extended all during the year. Also, there is an agreement as to the location of those campgrounds and picnic sites. It was an agreement between the federal government and the provincial governments that there would be one campground in each 100 miles and one picnic site in each 50 miles. There was one condition that the federal government put in at the beginning, namely that these campground sites along the trans-Canada highway would not be charged for, but some of the provinces objected; therefore, we mutually agreed last fall in a conference that there would be charges if the province wished. That is all the information I can give at the present time except possibly to say that four provinces have already completed some of their campgrounds and picnic sites. Those provinces are British Columbia, Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.

Mr. Chairman, I am concerned about the future of this particular program. In commenting earlier the minister told us that in 1958-59 the actual expenditures had been $1.72 million. Then, in 1959-60 the actual expenditures were $2.3 million.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: Estimated.

Estimated; the minister further told us that the program was going very well; that everyone was happy with it; that it should be a continuing program. Other hon. members have paid equal tribute to it. The hon. member for Wetaskiwin said that it is increasing yearly, as the figures which the minister gave us showed. The hon. member for Macleod told us that it is a program that hon. members think a lot of and that anyone who criticizes it, runs it down, or says that it is used for political purposes is out of order. What I should like to know, Mr. Chairman, is by what process of mental manipulation the minister arrives at the figure of $0.8 million as being required in the next fiscal year? Why would he anticipate that this program
Supply-Northern Affairs would be reduced to approximately one-third of the actual expenditures in 1959-60, when everyone has paid tribute to the fact that it is doing so well and is so well received in all parts of the country?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, probably the hon. member for Trinity was not here when I gave the explanation earlier. When we made up the estimates in the fall we had no way of knowing just what the provincial programs would consist of, and the figure of $0.8 million was put in for next year. Therefore, our supplementary estimates at this time of the year will take us up to March 31. We have a fairly good idea that the $800,000 we are voting now will cover us up to March 31 and that we have plans for this year's program right up to April and May, which we were pretty definite on, but you never know in the fall what the next program will come to.
Before I sit down, Mr. Chairman, I must inform the member for Macleod that I misinformed him. I said that the vote for the campgrounds and picnic sites on the trans-Canada highway was a separate item. The amounts are kept in a separate bookkeeping item, but actually the money comes out of the same item in the vote. I could have given this earlier but I did not notice it when I was answering the question. In the year 1958-59, out of a total of $1.72 million, $1.5 million was in the supplementaries for campgrounds and picnic sites, and there was no expenditure that first year along the trans-Canada highway. But in the second year, 1959-60, of the $2.3 million that is estimated up to the end of this March, $1.85 million of that was for campgrounds under the winter works program, and $0.45 million was for the trans-Canada highway. Therefore, there will be in this fiscal year roughly $500,000 spent. Next year, based on the submissions of the provinces so far, for the year starting April 1 and going into next year, $0.9 million is winter works and $0.8 million is trans-Canada highway. If the winter program is extended on into next year we may have a different vote. I have told the committee about the supplementaries, and these are the best estimates I have at the present time.
Did I understand the minister to say that the provinces were contributing 50-50 on the trans-Canada highway?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman.

Ninety per cent on some portions under the Liberal proposition.

Supply-Northern Affairs

The minister mentioned the participation of 10 provinces in the campground and picnic sites program. I wonder whether the minister would correct me if I am wrong. Does the government of the Yukon not also participate in this program with the federal government to establish campgrounds and picnic sites? If so, what was the federal participation last year and the year before?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: I apologize to the hon. member for Yukon. There is a program in the Yukon territory on a half and half basis. I was looking at the figures for campgrounds last night and along 500 to 600 miles of highway through the Yukon there are now campgrounds and picnic sites approximately every 41 miles on the average, which have been provided by the government at Ottawa and the territorial government. It is a very pleasant highway to drive along.

The minister has just said that this item of $800,000 in the final supplemen-taries, repeating what he said a few moments ago, is an item for the same program as the item of $800,000 in the main estimates which are also before us. He explained that the reason is that at the time the main estimates were drawn up the minister and the department did not have any exact knowledge of what money would be required under a program which, according to the minister, has been so successful. Surely the minister, knowing how much was to be spent in the current year through the main estimates and the final supplementaries-as a matter of fact, the total amount is $2,300,000-in the light of that information should have put more than $800,000 in the main estimates for the coming year. He has already told us also that he knows now that he is going to need another $900,000, almost $1 million. The Minister of Finance brings in his main estimates and makes a great play of the fact that he has reduced controllable expenditures but now we have learned that he has to add $1 million to his controllable expenditures next year because the minister is going to need nearly $1 million. He is going to need $900,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
I think that
opens up the whole issue of the last eight days. These expenditures are for the benefit of the unemployed. We have not been reducing these expenditures. There is the winter works program and as far as this general campground program is concerned we have offered to go as far as the provinces want to go. There is no limit. The provinces are still submitting programs for the coming fiscal year. I will not be able to tell the house for two or three months yet what the precise amount will be for the next fiscal year but I have tried to be frank with the committee and

give an idea of what the program was costing and what it was doing in a small way to help the unemployed during the winter months.
Can the minister say whether or not there is any limit on the amount of money that the government intends to recommend to parliament for this program? Is there any limit on the total amount?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
No, it is an
open end offer at the present time.

I wonder whether the minister would tell us what estimate he submitted to the treasury board last fall in the light of the fact he knew he was going to spend over $2 million. Is this just another case of that flimflam that the Minister of Finance gave us when he brought down the main estimates? In other words, the minister submitted an estimate of over $2 million and the Minister of Finance said, "We will knock $1 million off it now and you can bring it in under a supplementary". I think we ought to have the Minister of Finance here to tell us about this. He is the one who is responsible.
I understood the minister to say that he now knows that another $900,000 in addition to the $800,000 will have to be spent. Is that right?
That is what he said.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: The supplementary estimate with which we are dealing now is for $800,000 which takes us to the end of this month. We know that almost definitely within $4,000 or $5,000. At the time I made up my estimates last fall the estimated amount for the period March 31 to May 31 was $800,000. Since that time programs along the trans-Canada highway have come in on which we had no information at that time. I was quite frank with the committee tonight when I said that on the basis of present estimates it looks as though we will have to ask for approximately $900,000 in the supplementaries for 1960-61 but I will not know the correct amount until the provinces have completed the submission of their programs.

Mr. Chairman, I hope I am not out of order in speaking on item 618, but since the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam and the hon. member for Coast-Capilano brought up the question of the Olympics I should like to extend to all members of the House of Commons and to their wives and to their constituents an invitation to the world Olympics in 1968 at Banff, Alberta. At Banff, Alberta, we not only have

beauty but we do not have to build a mountain as would have to be done in Garibaldi park.
Does the hon. member know that he will not be around here in 1968?

Mr. Chairman, the minister just told us in his explanation, for which we thank him, that when he presented his estimate to treasury board and the Minister of Finance last fall he knew that an amount of approximately $800,000 would be required for the period from March 31 to May 31.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: No, I said that we estimated that the amount we would need from March 31 to May 31 for the coming fiscal year would be $800,000.

That is precisely the point. The minister is telling us that in these few months he expects he will spend $800,000 and yet this is an estimate put in the estimates tabled in the house for the whole fiscal year. The fiscal year of the government is not from March 31 to May 31; it is for 12 months. How can the minister come here and tell us that he is only making provision in what he is asking for in the main estimates for the period March 31 to May 31? Can he project on the basis of past experience approximately what he would expect to spend on this program for the full 12-month period?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman. There is a lack of comprehension on the part of some members of the opposition. The campground and picnic site program I am speaking about now has a winter works part to it which extends from November 1 to May 31 and covers part of two fiscal years. The program is decided each year on the basis of the unemployment situation. I am always hopeful that the program will be renewed next year but until it is renewed I cannot put an item in the main estimates.
Would the minister permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: I pointed out that under the same vote there is the other part having to do with trans-Canada highway picnic grounds which is an agreement that runs over the full 12 months for two years. If the provinces submit their estimates of work to be done under that program I can then calculate what I think I will need for the next year, and I have given the house tonight information that was not available four months ago.

The minister has made the precise point. He says that the part from March 31 to May 31 is the winter works part of the program. What about the money 79951-0-109
Supply-Northern Affairs that will have to be expended next fall from October until the following March? Is that not next year's winter works program and does the minister not anticipate at this time the necessity of having to carry on the program then, because he has told us it is open-ended? It is a blank cheque to the provinces. They can submit any number of projects and they will be approved. Can the minister not foresee the approximate extent of the program next winter in view of his experience in the last two years?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
I will try to spell it out in very simple terms for the hon. member. The program for the winter of
1960-61, the coming fall until the following spring, has not been decided on by the government and will not be until we have a picture of the unemployment situation next fall.

May I ask the minister
if what he is saying now is that the government does not know whether it is going to carry on this program in the winter of 1960-61? If so, where did he get the figure of $900,000 he was telling us about? Is that another $900,000 for March to May or is it just a figure he pulled out of his head?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: I must be having some trouble-
You are.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: -getting across to hon. gentlemen across the aisle a very simple proposition. First, the program of campgrounds and picnic sites to provide winter work runs from November 1 last to next May, and this vote is divided into two fiscal years. We know fairly definitely the amount of money we will need for this program and that has been indicated in the supplementary estimates we are dealing with now and the main estimates for next year. In addition to the winter works program, which is split into two fiscal years, there is a campground and picnic site program for the trans-Canada highway which works the full 12 months and which also covers two fiscal years.
But that expires December 31, 1960.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: I am not sure of the exact date, but I have to work the two programs into one vote. I think if hon. members just take it quietly and think about this for a while they will realize this is an accurate explanation.

I thank the minister for this further explanation, and I hope he now thoroughly understands his program.

Supply-Northern Affairs

The minister's explanation may be satisfactory to him, but how does he explain the fact that last year at this time there was a figure of $1.5 million in the main estimates, yet he has reduced that item of $1.5 million in the main estimates to a figure of $800,000 this year in connection with a program which was so successful? Last year, at this time in the main estimates there was $1.5 million and now he has $800,000. How does he explain that?

Is the minister not going to deal with the question asked by the Leader of the Opposition? Otherwise, the minister is obviously establishing the fact that he has agreed with the Minister of Finance, for the purpose of bookkeeping, to enable the Minister of Finance to give a false picture as to the financial situation in this country. The minister knows when these estimates are prepared what his requirements are. These supplementary estimates should have contained more, and this was an effort to assist the Minister of Finance in showing the government's expenditures for a given period are at a reduced level. Is this not so, and why does the minister not help the passage of this item by frankly admitting that was the real purpose behind this particular accounting method?
Order.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: I cannot cope with the hon. member for Essex East in his dialectical semantics.
Will the minister explain why he has reduced this item from $1.5 million to $800,000 this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: For the very clear reason, Mr. Chairman, that I go by the estimates of my officials, what they think the items will cost. If there was any such idea as that suggested by the hon. member for Essex East in our minds, then we obviously would not have made an open-ended deal, we would have closed it off.

I should like to ask the
minister a question. The minister says he requires another $800,000. Does the minister give us an undertaking that if this $800,000 were voted now, not one cent will be spent after March 31?
What are you trying to do, limit us?
No, I am just asking for information.

The minister has said this is an item which deals with unemployment, and that is why they are asking for this money. We have shown he reduced the estimate from


$1.5 million to $800,000 on an item which provides work, and he has no explanation for that reduction.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: I do not think we can let the hon. member get away with a thing like that.
There it is; there are the figures.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: The hon. member takes these two figures and draws his own conclusions from them. All I am going to point out is that I do the best I can with the information I have before me from each of the provinces. This is not the federal government doing the estimating, but the provinces submitting their intentions for the coming year. All I tried to do was make it clear to the committee the way the expenditures run in connection with this program. First of all, we do not actually know, at this time of year, what the final expenditures will be. No person does. This is the best estimate we have.

The minister is pointing out that notwithstanding his experience in the two previous years with this program, and knowing that, he estimated the expenditures for this year at just half what he estimated them a year ago, although the expenditures for a year ago had increased by 50 per cent over the estimate. Surely he does not expect the house to believe the explanation.
The Minister of Finance ought to be in here to face this.
He has not been here throughout the debate on unemployment.

It is not often I find myself in agreement with my hon. friends to the left. However, if we accept the argument of the minister we must, at the same time, completely reject the presentations made by hon. members from the various provinces across the country. We have been told by hon. members from various provinces across the country that this has been a very successful program, but a successful program is not curtailed, it is expanded. If we accept the explanation of the minister, the departmental officials in their wisdom and from their experience have cut this estimate in half which would mean that the program has not been successful and, therefore, they have cut it in half. We cannot have it both ways. Either the minister is right, and the recommendations of his department, or hon. members are definitely wrong in the picture they are painting. I think the minister should give a better explanation of this item than he has given so far.
In Quebec, it is about the same.

Item agreed to.
619. Acquisition of the pipelines (including the oil therein) and related facilities that are located in Canada and that belong to the United States government and form part of what is known as the Canol pipeline system, $670,000.
I would like to ask the minister exactly what facilities are being purchased, what facilities are covered by this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
I think the best way to handle this is to give briefly the story of the Canol pipeline system. During world war II, as a result of an agreement between the United States and Canada, four pipelines were constructed by the United States army in Canada. Canol pipelines, as these were called, consisted of four main divisions. Canol No. 1 was a four-inch line from Norman Wells to Whitehorse; Canol No. 2, a four-inch line from Skagway to Whitehorse; Canol No. 3, a two-inch line from Carcross to Watson Lake; Canol No. 4, a three-inch from Whitehorse to Fairbanks, Alaska.
The four-inch line, that is the line from Norman Wells to Whitehorse, was dismantled in 1947 by agreement between the two governments. The Canadian portion of the four-inch line from Skagway to Whitehorse was transferred to Canada in 1958, without a transfer payment as was specified in a note between the two countries. In 1958 the Alaska portion from Skagway to the Canadian border and the terminal pumping facilities at Skagway were transferred to the White Pass and Yukon Corporation by the United States army.
As a result of negotiations completed just recently between Canada and the United States it was agreed that the Canadian section of the three-inch line from Whitehorse up to Fairbanks, and the two-inch line from Car-cross down to Watson Lake, with all the appurtenant facilities of both lines, would be transferred to Canada effective February 29, 1960. This date has been changed just recently to March 31, 1960. We thought we would be at these estimates a little sooner. The compensation to be paid was based on an evaluation to be made by appraisers appointed by each government to determine the current market value of these assets. In their joint appraisal report of May, 1959, the appraisers estimated the current commercial value at $1,710,777.
Taking into consideration such factors as customs levies sales and income taxes and the release of the United States from certain obligations, it was agreed by Canada and the United States, as a result of a joint meeting on September 9, 1959, that the transfer price should be $617,021. In addition to the transfer 79951-0-109i
Supply-Northern Affairs price it was agreed that Canada should purchase the oil in the three-inch line at the date of transfer at cost plus a reasonable charge for handling. The value of this oil was calculated to be $51,920.40, United States funds. That is where the situation lies now.
The Canadian section from Carcross to Watson Lake and the Canadian section from Whitehorse to the United States boundary at Alaska is now being transferred to Canada. When the transfer is completed the government will have the question of disposition before it.

I have just one question by way of clarification. First, I want to thank the minister for the explanation he has given. But am I to understand from him there is no allowance made for customs and taxation in the item we are now voting and that it refers to payment to the United States plus payment for oil and certain other matters?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: Yes. The value, according to the appraiser was $1.7 million.
Yes; I heard that.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: But in the negotiations that followed the argument of the Canadian government was that this material had been brought in without custom duties, without sales tax and so on and therefore the price should be reduced. Also under the agreement the United States had certain obligations to Canada and we argued that in view of the fact they had not paid these taxes the price should be reduced to this figure you see in the estimates of $585,000 plus the cost of the oil, or a total figure of $670,000.
I wanted to be clear on that point. There is nothing in this item providing for charging any customs now that the Canadian government through the department is acquiring it.

I gather that this estimate is to pay for the completion of a series of transactions covering the Canol pipe line project going back a good many years and this particular transaction, I think the minister stated, covered Canol No. 4.
That is right.

Canol No. 4 and perhaps part of Canol No. 3. In any event, can the minister tell us when the earlier transaction was completed dealing with the other parts of the pipe line, the dates they were completed and the cost of the Canadian government in taking over the other parts of the line?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
The four-inch line from Norman Wells to Whitehorse was just dismantled so there is just no taking

Supply-Northern Affairs over there. That is the section from Mackenzie river up over the Mackenzie mountains down to Whitehorse. That was the four-inch line. Then as to Canol No. 2, the four-inch line from Skagway to Whitehorse via Car-cross, the Canadian portion of that line was transferred in 1958 without transfer payment as specified in paragraph 7 of the annex to the note 288, dated June 30, 1953. In 1958, as I said earlier, the Alaska portion from Skagway to the Canadian border and the terminal facilities at Skagway were transferred to the Whitepass and Yukon Corporation by the United States army. That was under the note of June 30, 1953. But the value of the balance, it was agreed, should be decided by these appraisers. Instead of it being $1.7 million, thanks to some very good bargaining on the part of some of our officials, the amount was reduced to approximately this figure of $700,000.
May I ask the minister why we took this line over at all? What value has this particular line to us?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: The first thing to remember about the line is that it is in use all the time. It is used to bring oil from Skagway up into Whitehorse following the right of way of the White Pass and Yukon Railway. It is also used-and we hope will be used- to run to the new refinery which is being built at Haines Junction. There is a new refinery there. I think it was built last year and it is in operation now. By taking over this line it is hoped we can work out eventually some deal that will bring cheaper fuel to the people of Yukon.

Having regard to the minister's remarks concerning the refinery at Haines Junction, is it contemplated in the transfer of the pipe line assets to the Canadian government that any subsequent arrangement is going to be made with the operators of this refinery in Haines Junction for transfer to them of these assets? Is the government in the course of negotiating with these people now for such a transfer or does the minister know whether any application has been made, for instance, to the board of transport commissioners for the operation of any line crossing the Alaska-Yukon boundary? While the minister is on his feet answering these questions perhaps he might inform me who the appraisers were who made the estimate of the value of the line being transferred.

Before the minister answers I wonder whether I might raise with him a very small matter? In his answer a moment ago to the Leader of the Opposition I believe he stated that part of this line being
[Mr. Hamilton (Qu'Appelle) .1

purchased under this item was used to transport oil from Skagway to Whitehorse. I think that is not what he intended to say. As I understood his earlier remark, the part being purchased under this item is the part from Whitehorse extending to the Alaska boundary. I just wanted clarification of that point.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
Yes. There is no difference between us. The first part from the Canadian border to Whitehorse was taken over last summer or at least in 1958. It is being operated at the present time by White Pass and Yukon. The two lines we are taking over are one from Whitehorse to the Alaska and Yukon boundary, and the other pipe line running down via Carcross to Watson lake. The hon. member for Yukon asked about the disposition.
These matters are now before the government. At the present time White Pass and Yukon, is operating the section from Skagway through to Whitehorse and the refining company has asked that they may take over the line that runs up to the Alaska border. That is as much as I can say at the present time.

The reason I asked, of course, is that I understand-although I may be incorrect in this understanding-that White Pass and Yukon who operate that section of the line from Skagway to Whitehorse supply petroleum products now to Yukon and they offered, I believe, to the board of transport commissioners two and a half or three years ago to operate the line as a common carrier; that is to say, if another firm or petroleum distributor wishes to come into the area to compete with White Pass they could do so as a common carrier with that line. I raise this point because I think some people fear that should there be placed in operation another supplier of petroleum products, another line into the Yukon, this may have an effect opposite to that of saving the user of petroleum products in the Yukon any money.
I wonder whether the minister can assure the committee now whether it is the intention to place this matter-namely the matter of the possibility of a transfer of this facility to any other petroleum distributor intending to operate either in Yukon or Alaska-before the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
The point raised by the hon. member for Yukon has not been considered by me or the government but I will take it under advisement because we still have the disposition of these pipe lines to decide.

I was asked a question as to who are the appraisers. The names I have here are Mr. J. Bland of Defence Production for Canada and Mr. Darnielle, a United States professional appraiser. I do not know his initials.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened with great interest to the explanation of the minister to the purchase of this pipe line by the government, but I am not very clear yet as to the reason the government purchased it. Why did they purchase it if there are private interests who want to operate and rent it? By purchasing it in this way they are just assuming a liability which otherwise would have been assumed by private interests. Now they have purchased it, why are they not considering operating it as a crown corporation? We would like a further explanation as to the reason the government intends to spend $670,000 of this country's money on the purchase of this pipe line, while at the same time, according to the minister's remarks, he seemed very vague as to the disposition of the property after it is purchased.

Mr. Chairman, before the minister makes a reply to the hon. member for Kootenay West may I place on record my very violent opposition to any suggestion that the pipe lines in the Yukon be operated by a crown corporation. The White Pass and Yukon route have been in operation there for some 60 years and depend to a very large extent for their existence on the operation of the petroleum distribution system. Any detraction from their position by the government coming in and competing with them and controlling the supply and distribution would, I am afraid, severely interrupt, if not bring about a cessation of their over-all operation of shipping; their railroading and trucking operations throughout the whole of the Yukon territory. They have built it up over the years and one of the mainstays of the operation is the petroleum distribution business, so any competition in this way by a crown corporation would be quite unacceptable.

Mr. Chairman, before the minister answers I would also like to add my voice to that of the hon. member for the Yukon. I believe we have too many crown companies now and this is a way by which on government can take over from another government commonly owned assets. There should be a transitional stage and it should then be turned over to some private operator up there who can operate it under our free enterprise system. Let us keep the crown out of this.

Mr. Chairman, I was wondering if the hon. member for Qu'Appelle had
Supply-Northern Affairs anything further to add to what the minister from the Yukon has just said. I am interested to know why we are spending $670,000 of public money when apparently the minister said today, and as the hon. member for the Yukon added by way of further explanation, that it is intended to turn the property over to a private company, although at the present time the disposition of the property is not quite certain. What is the reason for purchasing this property when at the present time the government does not even know what its disposition will be?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the answer is quite simple. The lines were built in 1942, and as part of the agreement Canada agreed to purchase these facilities when the war should end. Negotiations started shortly after the war, were carried on and are now completed.

Mr. Chairman, I think this is hardly good enough. The minister is now asking us to spend almost $1 million of the taxpayer's money to buy something which, if I gauge his remarks rightly, he intends to hand over to private enterprise immediately afterwards. I think it is hardly good enough to ask the taxpayers of Canada to bail out something that is obviously bankrupt at the present time in order to make it available to private enterprise to make some money. I object very strenuously to this.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not want to leave that wild thought floating around this chamber. It is not for me to say whether this Canol pipe line was a wise thing to undertake during the war years, but I would like to point out to the committee that it cost several hundred millions of dollars and the United States put up all the money. If after this tremendous expenditure we end up with the useful parts of the line for a sum of a little over half a million dollars I do not think the taxpayers can feel they have had a bad deal.
Will the minister assure the house that if the property is sold for private interests the taxpayer will not lose more than this estimate, or whatever the cost is?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
The minister will guarantee that whatever arrangement is made it will be on the basis of a common carrier provision in the agreement to make sure that any company can use these lines. Second, the decision which the government will make, I am sure, will be based on finding ways and means of bringing the lowest priced fuel to this newly developed part of Canada.	.

Mr. Chairman, is it not a fact that any disposition of these lines must be handled through the board of transport commissioners, so that the government cannot give any guarantee as to it being a common carrier?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: I think the hon. member may be right, Mr. Chairman. Applications probably have to be made to the board of transport commissioners, but I would also remind him that at the present time, if this item goes through, we can pay off the United States and then transfer it over as of March 31. Then we will be owners of the appurtenances and will have some say in the matter.

Will the minister explain why it is necessary for the government to enter that arrangement at all, if private enterprises are expected to be the operators? The sum of $1 million does not mean much to oil companies, so why should not they be the people who do the buying? Why does the taxpayer have to foot the bill in the first place?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: There is a very simple reason. This is an agreement between two sovereign nations and the agreement has to be completed by Canada fulfilling its obligation of purchasing the facilities. Once the facilities are purchased then it becomes a matter within the country and we will take the necessary steps to make such disposition as is fair and reasonable.

I would like to ask whether agreements are already in existence whereby the government agrees, once they have concluded the purchase, to resell this pipe line to individual interests and, if so, what are the terms of the agreement?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: There is no such agreement, Mr. Chairman.
